documents: Rhoades et al. 2022, Nature Climate Change 12, 1151-1159, published PDF (12 pages including Methods)
Publisher full text from XML with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

entry.evidence: It is therefore imperative to understand and estimate how these process interactions influence the emergence of a low-to-no-snow future across the American Cordillera

sequences.source_document: Rhoades et al. 2022, Nature Climate Change (published text, XML and PDF)

steps.action: The authors take from palaeoclimate, historical and model literature the expectation that climate-change responses may be asymmetric between hemispheres, through circulation, thermodynamic and hypsometric processes.
steps.quote: there is evidence in the palaeoclimate and historical record that hemispheric changes induced by climate change may be asymmetric

steps.action: The authors pose the question of when, and at what warming level, low-to-no-snow conditions emerge in each midlatitude hemisphere of the American Cordillera.
steps.quote: the emergence of low-to-no-snow conditions may occur at different times in the midlatitudes of the northern and southern hemispheres

steps.action: The authors choose the existing high-resolution HighResMIP ensemble under SSP5-8.5 because coarse Earth system models cannot resolve mountain snowpack.
steps.quote: we leverage the High Resolution Model Intercomparison Project (HighResMIP) ensemble43, which utilizes the high-emissions (SSP5-8.5) scenario44

steps.action: The authors adopt published definitions: the Körner mountain mask for the Cordillera and the Siirila-Woodburn peak-SWE percentile definition of low-to-no snow.
steps.quote: [...] örner et al.45 in defining mountains, particularly the American Cordillera, and Siirila-Woodburn et al.16 in quantitatively characterizing low-to-no-snow emergence.

steps.action: In the Methods, the authors compare the 20 km model's latitudinal elevation with the Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment; the mean matches and the maximum has a ~1,000 m low bias.
steps.quote: has nearly the same representation of the mean latitudinal elevation (between 28 m and 3,497 m) as the Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment

steps.action: The authors map latitude-band peak-SWE percentiles over 1950-2100 and establish a weak signal-to-noise ratio before 2050 and consistent below-median snow after 2050.
steps.quote: After 2050, below-median historical peak SWE percentiles are consistently projected across the American Cordillera, indicating a stronger signal-to-noise emergence

steps.action: From the diverging hemispheric warming and the weakening northern meridional overturning circulation (Fig. 2), the authors propose that emergence is dynamically and thermodynamically driven in the north and mainly thermodynamically driven in the south.
steps.quote: In the southern hemisphere, the general circulation shows little response to warming, and low-to-no-snow emergence could be controlled primarily through thermodynamic controls.

steps.action: The authors compare mean peak-SWE changes across six HighResMIP simulations; results are inconsistent for 2015-2050, but both models running to 2100 show declines in both hemispheres.
steps.quote: a notable decrease in mean peak SWE in both hemispheres is found by the two models that project out to 2100

steps.action: Because the multi-model view cannot isolate emergence, the authors narrow the analysis to the 20 km MRI-AGCM3-2-S 150-year run. They fix a ≤30th-percentile threshold, extreme, episodic and persistent durations, and symmetric ±32-59° latitude bands.
steps.quote: it does not enable precise isolation of the emergence and persistence of snow loss

steps.action: The authors fit logistic regressions of binary low-to-no-snow occurrence on surface air temperature for each latitude band and take the first year with probability >0.5 as the date of emergence. Southern extreme emergence comes 17 years earlier (2039 vs 2056).
steps.quote: The hemispheric-wide emergence of extreme low-to-no-snow conditions occurs 17 years earlier in the southern hemisphere

steps.action: The authors vary the duration threshold (extreme, episodic, persistent) and find that the hemispheric asymmetry persists (17, 19 and 22 years).
steps.quote: This midlatitude asymmetry in low-to-no-snow emergence timing is approximately the same for the episodic threshold (with a hemispheric difference of 19 years)

steps.action: Given the convergence of episodic and persistent dates, the authors define post-emergence as all years after episodic emergence (2051 south, 2070 north).
steps.quote: post-emergence of low-to-no snow is hereafter defined as all years following the emergence of episodic low-to-no snow

steps.action: The authors compare the model's faster northern-hemisphere warming with published studies of interhemispheric temperature asymmetry and find it consistent.
steps.quote: The northern hemisphere, consistent with Xu and Ramanathan27 and Friedman et al.28, warms faster than the southern hemisphere (Fig. 2a)

steps.action: The authors estimate the warming at emergence: local +3.5 °C (north) versus +1.2 °C (south), and global +3.5 to 4.1 °C versus +2.4 to 2.9 °C. They also report asymmetric elevation-dependent warming.
steps.quote: In the southern hemisphere, this occurs with approximately a third of the local warming

steps.action: The authors explain the warming-level difference partly by the historically warmer southern mountain climatology.
steps.quote: This difference is partly explained by the historically warmer local annual surface air temperatures in the mountainous regions of the southern hemisphere

steps.action: The authors quantify post-emergence changes in temperature, precipitation, snowfall fraction, rain on bare ground and freezing days by latitude band.
steps.quote: the net decline in snowfall fraction is comparable (median of −42%) following the emergence of low-to-no snow

steps.action: The authors quantify historical and post-emergence runoff efficiency: a consistent northern decline (−11%) and a heterogeneous southern response split near 44° S.
steps.quote: Post-emergence of low-to-no snow, the northern midlatitudes exhibit a consistent decrease in runoff efficiency (median of −11%)

steps.action: The authors compare the simulated earlier peak SWE and slower snowmelt with published findings and report agreement.
steps.quote: corroborating the findings of Trujillo and Molotch52 and Musselman et al.53

steps.action: The authors propose glacial decline and/or extreme storms as the cause of the runoff-efficiency increase above 3,000 m in the south, without testing it.
steps.quote: We hypothesize that this is probably a signature of glacial decline and/or extreme storm events

steps.action: The authors map end-of-century runoff-efficiency changes, separately for low-snow/low-precipitation years and for high-precipitation years.
steps.quote: Runoff efficiency also decreases during future wet years (Fig. 5d,h)

steps.action: The authors keep the claim of asymmetric emergence (2070 at +3.5 °C local in the north, 2051 at +1.2 °C in the south) and conclude that global warming must stay at or below +2.5 °C.
steps.quote: Our findings suggest that the prevention of midlatitude low-to-no snow emergence requires global warming to be limited to, at most, +2.5 °C.

steps.action: Using the supplement, the authors compare the model's historical climatology with reanalyses and gridded observations, its climate sensitivity with other HighResMIP models, and its emergence timing with NA- and SA-CORDEX downscaling.
steps.quote: the historical climatology was wetter and colder than several reanalysis datasets and regional observation-based gridded products

steps.action: The authors qualify the warming-level estimate as probably conservative (emergence may come earlier) because of the model's cold, wet bias and low climate sensitivity.
steps.quote: the global warming level that gives rise to low-to-no snow emergence may be a conservative estimate

tree.answer: Projected emergence of widespread, persistent low-to-no snow; weak signal-to-noise before 2050
No; seen only in model projections, not in observations
Estimate the date and warming level of emergence for each hemisphere
No formal rivals; dynamical, thermodynamic and hypsometric factors proposed as joint contributors
No distinct predictions derived for the competing mechanisms
Conditions found in one existing SSP5-8.5 simulation, not set
Partly: holds across duration thresholds and is qualitatively consistent with two 2100 models and CORDEX, but single model and single member
Kept as an estimate with confidence intervals, flagged as conservative

end.claim: In MRI-AGCM3-2-S under SSP5-8.5, low-to-no snow emerges about 20 years earlier in the southern than the northern midlatitudes of the American Cordillera (2051 vs 2070), at about a third of the local warming (+1.2 vs +3.5 °C); preventing it requires global warming of at most +2.5 °C.

decisive_move.sentence: The logistic-regression estimate of the date and degrees of emergence for each latitude band of the 20 km MRI-AGCM3-2-S run produces the asymmetry and the warming-level threshold.

gates.evidence: The asymmetry expectation (§1 ¶4-5) directed the choice of the Cordillera and of symmetric ±32-59° bands (§2 ¶4; §5.2 ¶1), but the data are an existing HighResMIP ensemble that was not acquired for the test. The asymmetry could have failed to appear, and the threshold variation and multi-model and CORDEX comparisons expose it partly; no rival prediction was stated. The ≤30th-percentile definition was taken from prior published work (Siirila-Woodburn et al. 2021; §5.3 ¶2), but the duration definitions, latitude bands and 0.5 probability threshold are not stated as fixed before the output was examined.

imports.item: Logistic regression of binary occurrence on temperature, with a 0.5 probability threshold for emergence
Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment mountain mask (Körner et al.)
Duration thresholds (extreme, episodic, persistent) based on historical water-management impacts and storage capacity

novelty_claims.quote: Because it is one of the first multi-model ensembles that provide simulations at resolutions needed to capture global-scale [...]
we note that our analysis is a proof of concept of what future high-resolution multi-model ensembles could deliver

limits: The headline estimate rests on a single-member, single-model, single-scenario simulation (§5.1 ¶3), so the confidence intervals reflect spread across latitude bands, not structural or internal-variability uncertainty. Sub-claims at other statuses: the mechanistic attribution (northern circulation slowdown versus southern thermodynamic control; hypsometry) is at most best_explanation, proposed from Fig. 2 without a discriminating test. The glacial-decline explanation of high-elevation southern runoff increases is an untested hypothesis (none). Runoff-efficiency declines are estimate_with_resolution without uncertainty bounds. The +2.5 °C threshold inherits the single-model limitation, and the authors call it conservative. Coding the narrowing to MRI-AGCM3-2-S as return_after_failure is an inference from the statement that Fig. 1 cannot isolate emergence. Several checks (reanalysis comparison, climate sensitivity, CORDEX, multi-model maps) sit in a supplement that was not supplied, so their content is coded from main-text statements only. No peer-review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded and tree question 9 is not answered, although the paper names four referees. Composition is none_fits: the walk is a model-output estimation with no rivals, no new capability and no frozen forecast; the closest is an estimation from a found simulation. The first novelty quote refers to the HighResMIP ensemble, not to the authors' own analysis; the paper makes no explicit 'first' claim about its own results.

disagreements.support: The authors argue that drought implies a temporary deviation, which is inappropriate under continuous warming, and substitute the low-to-no snow term with analogous thresholds.
disagreements.quote: we opt for the low-to-no snow terminology because drought implies a temporary deviation from average that is unlikely to occur in a continuously warming world

disagreements.target: Fixed calendar dates (for example, 1 April) used in resource management
disagreements.support: The authors argue that fixed dates cannot track earlier peak-SWE timing with warming or apply across hemispheres, and use peak SWE instead.
disagreements.quote: gets around arbitrary dates often used in resource management (for example, 1 April) that cannot account for earlier shifts in peak SWE timing with warming

disagreements.target: Rain-snow partitioning in most Earth system models (temperature only)
disagreements.support: Citing Jennings et al., the authors note that relative humidity shifts the rain-snow threshold, which the chosen model includes and most models omit.
disagreements.quote: MRI-AGCM3-2 relies on both surface air temperature and, unlike most Earth system models, relative humidity to determine rain–snow partitioning

disagreements.target: Infrastructure design and management strategies assuming climate stationarity
disagreements.support: The authors cite palaeoclimate records and projections, plus their own projected runoff declines, as inconsistent with stationarity assumptions.
disagreements.quote: infrastructure design and management strategies that have largely assumed climate stationarity and that do not agree with palaeoclimate records or future climate projections
